title: Regret and rank plot across test problems: which optimizer is best on average?
summary: To say which optimizer is best on average, run them on many test problems, rank them on each, and compare the mean ranks. A critical-difference diagram draws the mean ranks on one axis and joins the optimizers that are not significantly different.

media.alt: A critical-difference diagram: a horizontal rank axis from 1 to 5 with a scale bar labelled CD = 1.76 above it, five optimizers hanging from their mean ranks (A 1.58, B 2.50, C 2.67, D 3.58, E 4.67), and three teal horizontal bars below joining A, B and C; B, C and D; D and E.
media.caption: Reference render of class F7.10 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Which optimizer is best on average?
read_the_figure.axes: A single horizontal axis: mean rank over 12 test problems, 1 (best) on the left to 5 (worst) on the right. Optimizer names with their mean ranks hang from the axis on the left and right. A bar of length CD sits above the axis; thick bars below connect groups.
look_at: Which optimizers are joined by a bar: those cannot be told apart at this sample size.
How long is the CD bar relative to the spread of the ranks?
Which optimizer is significantly better than which (a gap larger than CD)?
How many test problems and which test and level define CD?
as_drawn: Five optimizers over 12 test problems. Mean ranks: A 1.58, B 2.50, C 2.67, D 3.58, E 4.67 (they sum to 15, as ranks of five items must).
The critical difference is CD = 1.76 (shown by the amber bar), from the Nemenyi test at 0.05 with k = 5 and N = 12.
Three bars join A with B and C, B and C with D, and D with E. So A is significantly better than D and E, and B and C are better than E, while neighbours are not distinguishable.
The title says regret and rank plot, but only the rank part is drawn: the amount of regret is not shown, so a large win and a tiny win count equally.
read_the_figure.proves: With these 12 problems, a gap in mean rank larger than CD is unlikely to arise by chance among equivalent optimizers. Joined optimizers are not shown to be equivalent: with so few problems the test lacks power.
if_wrong: Mean ranks that do not sum to k(k+1)/2: a ranking mistake or ties handled inconsistently.
CD stated without k, N or the test: the bar cannot be checked.
Bars drawn between optimizers whose gap exceeds CD: an error in the clique construction.
must_check: critical-difference marks: a ranking without a significance yardstick invites the reader to read noise as differences.

terms.meaning: The position of an optimizer on one problem, 1 for the best.
The average rank of an optimizer over all test problems.
A non-parametric test of whether the mean ranks of several methods differ over several problems.
The smallest gap in mean rank that the Nemenyi post-hoc test calls significant.
How much worse an optimizer's result is than the best result on that problem.
A group of optimizers joined by a bar because none of their gaps exceeds CD.

remember: CD = q_alpha sqrt(k (k + 1) / (6 N)); here q = 2.728, k = 5, N = 12 gives 1.76.
Ranks of k methods sum to k (k + 1) / 2 on each problem.
A gap larger than CD is significant; a bar means no gap exceeds CD.
Ranks ignore the size of the differences.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position along the horizontal axis is the mean rank, so better optimizers sit to the left. Each optimizer hangs from its position by an elbow line and is labelled with its rank. The amber bar above the axis has the length of the critical difference on the same scale. Thick teal bars below join optimizers whose gaps are all smaller than that length.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: on one problem the best optimizer may be luck, so the question is which is better in general. Ranking them on each problem removes the scale of the objective and gives every problem equal say. Averaging the ranks and drawing a ruler that is as long as the smallest meaningful gap tells you which differences to believe: anything inside a bar is not established.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Ranks discard the size of the differences: an optimizer that wins by a hair on every problem ranks the same as one that wins by orders of magnitude. The Nemenyi test is conservative and the bars can be intransitive (A joined to B, B to C, but A not joined to C). With 12 problems a joined pair may well be different but untested. And the result applies only to the test suite chosen. In this render the regret part promised by the title is not drawn.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A performance profile (the fraction of problems solved within a factor of the best cost) keeps the size of the differences. A table of the mean rank with a pairwise test for the best method against each other with a correction is another option. A race on a single problem (F7.1) gives the details behind one rank.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a panel of the regret (the log of the ratio to the best) as boxes per optimizer, print k, N, alpha and the Friedman statistic in the caption, and show the diagram for N = 24 problems to see CD shrink.

steps.title: Critical difference
steps.note: The Nemenyi critical value q for k = 5 and alpha = 0.05 is 2.728; verified numerically against the studentised range distribution.

steps.title: Friedman test
steps.note: With four degrees of freedom this gives p of about 3e-5, so the optimizers differ overall; CD says which pairs.

steps.title: Gaps against CD
steps.note: A and D are significantly different, A and C are not; this is what the bars in the render show.

worked.title: Reading the critical-difference diagram of the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What is the critical difference and how is it obtained? (2) Which pairs involving A are significantly different? (3) How would CD change with 24 problems?

solution.text: (1) From the formula with k = 5, N = 12 and q = 2.728.
(2) Gaps from A (1.58): B 0.92, C 1.09 (both below 1.76: not significant), D 2.00 and E 3.09 (both above: significant).
(3) CD falls as one over the square root of N.

worked.answer: CD = 1.76; A is significantly better than D and E but not than B or C; with 24 problems CD would shrink to 1.25 and more pairs would separate.

analyze.q: B and C are both joined to D but A is not joined to D. Is that a contradiction?
Why can ranks hide the size of an advantage?
analyze.hint: Two methods with a hairline and a huge win rank the same.

analyze.q: What would you do to make the diagram more informative about regret?
analyze.hint: A second panel with the size of the differences.

evaluate.q: A is ranked first. Would you use it for your own problem?
evaluate.hint: Is your problem like the test problems? Budget? Joined optimizers.

Add a performance profile beside the diagram to show how much better the winner is.

checks.q: What does a bar joining two optimizers mean?
checks.answer: That the difference of their mean ranks is smaller than the critical difference, so the data do not show them to be different.

checks.q: Why is a gap slightly larger than CD not proof that one optimizer is better in general?
checks.answer: The test applies only to the chosen problems; a gap just above CD is borderline at the 5 percent level and may not hold on other problems; ranks also hide the size of the gap.
